summary: Records the ideas, good and bad, of Pip, a proposed next-generation Internet protocol, in the near-term architecture. It is a companion to RFC 1622. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Notes about an idea for a new Internet design that was not adopted. They are kept so people can learn from it.

questions: what is a pip header server
why was pip merged into sipp
subtitle: A record of Pip, a candidate replacement for IPv4 with hierarchical provider-based addresses and IDs kept separate from addresses.

tldr.problem: In 1992 and 1993 the Internet needed a replacement for IP version 4 that scaled better, supported rich routing and could evolve without replacing every host at once.
tldr.mechanism: Pip separates a host's identity (a 64-bit Pip ID) from its location (a hierarchical, provider-rooted Pip Address), carries addresses as a chain of 16-bit fields, and adds a Pip Header Server, DNS extensions and a Pip Control Message Protocol around them.
tldr.outcome: Pip was merged with the Simple Internet Protocol to form SIPP, which kept the identifier/address split and source routing but dropped many other Pip ideas. This RFC preserves the rest, and it is Historic.

today: RFC 1621 is Historic. The Pip project ended when Pip was merged with SIP to form SIPP, and this RFC records its ideas rather than specifying a protocol. Its header details are in the companion RFC 1622.

sections.title: The Near-Term Pip Architecture
sections.content:
Pip was an internet protocol developed at Bellcore and intended as the replacement for IP version 4. In mid 1993 it was merged with the Simple Internet Protocol (SIP) to create SIPP, and the preamble of this RFC says its purpose is to record the ideas, good and bad, of Pip. Any text that presents Pip as the intended replacement for IP should be ignored.

The near-term architecture is described as an incremental step from IP. It is a datagram protocol that runs under TCP and UDP, uses DNS to distribute name to address and ID mappings, and routes hop by hop, although a host may build a domain-level source route for policy reasons. Its main difference from IP is that addresses have more hierarchy, are provider-based, and are assigned to hosts and routers automatically.

The architecture has five systems: hosts, routers, DNS, the Pip/IP Translator (needed only to interoperate with IP, and built into every Pip router) and the new Pip Header Server, which formats Pip headers on behalf of a source host.
sections.plainLanguage: Pip is a blueprint for a bigger and smarter version of the Internet's addressing system. It keeps the same basic delivery style as the old one but adds helpers, such as a server that writes the address labels for you.

sections.title: The Pip Header in Brief
sections.content:
The Pip header has three parts: an Initial Part, a Transit Part and an Options Part. The Initial Part is fixed in length at 8 32-bit words. It holds the version number, option bookkeeping, a Packet SubID, the Protocol, the Dest ID and Source ID, the Payload Length, a Host Version, a Payload Offset and a Hop Count (similar to IP's Time-to-Live).

The Transit Part carries what routers need. The Handling Directive (HD) triggers handling such as queueing priority or drop priority and never affects routing. The Routing Directive holds a Routing Context (RC) and a chain of 16-bit Forwarding Table Index Fields (FTIFs). A router uses the RC to pick one of several forwarding tables and then indexes the table with the active FTIF.

Evolution is built in. The HD, the RC and the options each have a Contents field that says which parameters are present, and its meaning is configured manually. Systems that do not understand a new parameter can be set to ignore it, set it to all 0s or all 1s, silently discard the packet, or discard it with a PCMP message. The details of the header are left to the companion document, RFC 1622.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet has a label with three parts: the basic facts, the part routers read to decide where to send it, and optional extras. The label can be redesigned over time because it says which kind of label it is.

sections.title: Pip Addresses and Pip IDs
sections.content:
Pip separates who a host is from where it is. The Pip ID is 64 bits long, is treated as flat, and identifies the source and destination host. A Pip Address is used only for routing. It is written as a series of numbers, one per level of the hierarchy, and is provider-rooted: the top level names a network service provider. The basic form is providerPart,subscriberPart, and a host reachable through several providers can have several addresses that share one subscriber part.

Because each level is its own 16-bit FTIF, no field-size decisions are needed, and a router can often forward on a single level of the address. FTIF values 0 to 31 are reserved. A root authority (IANA or ISOC are named as likely choices) assigns top-level numbers, and the text says roughly 32,000 top-level assignments can be made before the FTIF size must grow from 16 bits to 32 bits.

Bits 0 and 1 of the Routing Context select one of four address families: hierarchical unicast, Class D style multicast, CBT style multicast (a single tree rooted at a core router) and anycast (route to the nearest of a group). When a packet reaches the last router, it uses the Dest ID, with ARP if needed, to find the host on its subnetwork.
sections.plainLanguage: Your Pip ID is like your name, which stays the same. Your Pip Address is like your street address, which changes when you move. Keeping them apart means people can still reach you.

sections.title: DNS, the Header Server and Host Mobility
sections.content:
In a typical exchange the application gives a destination domain name to the Pip Header Server, which asks DNS and gets back a Pip ID, several Pip Addresses and possibly a mobile host server or a PDN address. It then returns an ordered list of valid Pip headers to the host. If the server runs on the host, the host behaves much like an IP host doing a DNS lookup. The Pip Header Protocol (PHP) is a simple query and response protocol for this exchange.

Pip addresses are expected to change more often than IP addresses. To still allow aggressive DNS caching, the network tells a host when an address is known to be invalid, using a PCMP Packet Not Delivered message, and the host then makes an authoritative query.

Mobility is confined to hosts. A mobile host puts its new Pip Address in its next packet. If both ends move at once, they ask each other's Mobile Host Server, using a PCMP Mobile Host message with a sequence number and a signature field. The encryption used for the signature is left for further study, and the RFC admits that its anti-spoofing measures are no more secure than DNS itself.

The Pip Control Message Protocol (PCMP) is Pip's analog to ICMP, with 11 message types defined in this architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending, your computer asks a helper for the right address labels. If you move house, you just tell your friends your new address, or leave it with a friend who always knows where you are.

sections.title: Routing and Exit Providers
sections.content:
Routing is split by level of the address hierarchy, much like the split between exterior and interior routing in IP but at every level. At the top level Pip uses a path-vector algorithm, based on IDRP and called MLPV (Multi-Level Path-Vector). Below the top level it is a local decision which algorithm runs, and MLPV can also serve as the interface between different routing technologies.

To keep track of which level a packet is at, the Routing Context holds a level and a metalevel. A metalevel boundary exists wherever an element may have parents with different numbers of levels, for example between a subscriber and its provider.

A private domain can choose its provider in two ways. With host-driven exit routing the source host picks the provider. With transit-driven exit routing the routers choose, and a border router can redirect the host with a PCMP Provider Redirect message. Routers exchange only the levels they need, so a subscriber router often does not need provider-internal routes.
sections.plainLanguage: Big cities pick the highways between them, and each neighborhood picks its own streets. A traveler can either choose which highway to leave by or let the road signs decide.

sections.title: Transition from IP and Autoconfiguration
sections.content:
The transition plan has two parts: translation between Pip and IP addresses, and encapsulation, where Pip systems tunnel through IP routers and treat IP as a link layer. The Pip hop count is not copied into the IP Time-to-Live. The RFC argues against relying on NAT, though it notes NAT could be added later if needed. Pip IDs can embed a 32-bit IP address, so translating Pip to IP is straightforward, while IP to Pip needs a DNS-based table. DNS is extended with new resource records and a new opcode, so a resolver can tell whether a name server is Pip-capable.

Old TCP binaries are handled by making the pseudo-header checksum come out right: when both Pip IDs are IP-based only the 32-bit IP address is used, otherwise all 64 bits are used.

Autoconfiguration is meant to keep manual setup to DNS and border routers. A host builds a flat Pip ID locally, for example from an IEEE 802 number, learns its Pip Addresses from router discovery, and can optionally obtain a domain name from an ID/domain name assignment service at a well-known anycast address. The design of that service is left for further study. The RFC states that security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: To switch to a new addressing system without breaking the old one, the new system can ride inside the old one like a letter inside a bigger envelope, and translators swap labels at the border.
